reconcile.connective: Harmonizers read the Mosaic ban as not covering Moabite women, and treat Ruth as a converted proselyte exempt from it.

discrepancy.connective: André LaCocque argues the book of Ruth is a deliberate counter-narrative to the post-exilic intermarriage purge of Ezra-Nehemiah, celebrating as the conduit of David's line the very Moabite union those texts condemn.

skeptic.name: André LaCocque
skeptic.attribution: André LaCocque, Ruth: A Continental Commentary (Fortress Press, 2004)

excerpts.excerpt_text: The law of Moses had prohibited the Moabites, even to the tenth generation, from entering into the congregation of the Lord; but this law, the Jews think, did not extend to women; and even if it had, Ruth's might be considered an exempt case, as she had been already incorporated into the family by marriage; and left her own country, people, and gods, to become a proselyte to the true God in the land of Israel.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Clarke names the exact Deuteronomy 23 prohibition the contradiction turns on and offers the two stock harmonizations (the ban excludes women; Ruth is an exempt proselyte) for why Boaz's Moabite marriage was lawful.

pd_work.resource: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832), note on Ruth 4:13
pd_work.author: Adam Clarke
pd_work.note: Clarke addresses this passage directly, arguing the Deuteronomy 23:3 ban on Moabites did not extend to women and that Ruth, as a proselyte already incorporated by marriage, was an exempt case.
